totpOff1: The authentication policy turns authenticator apps off (
totpOff2: ), so nobody new can enrol an authenticator app. It does not disable a secret somebody already holds — that account is still configured for two factors and the sign-in screen still asks for the code, because a switch that silently downgraded it would be a security control whose off position does something other than what it says. Clearing an existing enrolment is on that person's row under
totpCode: {digits} digits, a new one every {period} seconds
totpSkew: {window} step(s) either side, so a code lives about {life} seconds. This one applies to everybody, existing enrolments included.
bcOfferedYes: — a set is issued the first time somebody enrols a second factor.
bcOfferedNo: — no NEW set will be issued. A set already issued goes on working, which is the contract the authentication policy's TOTP row and webauthn.enabled both keep: a switch that took away the only way back into an account whose phone is lost would be the worst one on this console.
bcSet: {count} codes of {length} characters, printed in groups of {group}.
bcStrength: {bits} bits per code, out of an alphabet of {alphabet}. That is the number that matters rather than the length, and it is what makes the rate limit on the recovery screen a belt rather than the whole trousers.
bcAlphabet1: — the same thirty-two characters RFC 4648 base32 uses, and
bcAlphabet2: . That one is base32 because the otpauth URI says so; this one is these characters because no pair of them is confusable — no 0 beside O, no 1 beside I — and a recovery code is the one credential here that somebody writes on paper and types back months later.
bcCompared: Every code in the set is compared even after a match, so the time taken does not depend on WHICH one matched.
bcWillNotHeading: What this service will not do with them
bcNoteRequest: There is no control anywhere that issues a set on request. Not on this console, not on /admin-api, not on /portal. A set is created by the ACT of enrolling a second factor and by nothing else, because a way back that somebody has to remember to ask for produces exactly the population it exists to protect — the people who did not ask are the people who will need it.
bcNoteOnce1: A set is issued ONCE and is never topped up. Enrolling a different second factor does not reissue: somebody who printed a list in March and replaced their authenticator app in June would otherwise be holding a page of strings that had stopped working with nothing having said so. The only route to a second set is an operator's Clear on that person's row under
bcNoteOnce2: , after which the next enrolment issues one.
bcNoteNeverShown: This console never shows a code. The person reads their own set back on /portal/mfa and nowhere else. Showing them here would hand a working second factor to whoever holds Admin Read, which is the same door this console already refuses to open for an authenticator enrolment.
bcNoteNotFirst: A recovery code is never a FIRST factor and never the factor a sign-in asks for. credentials.mechanismsFor().secondFactor answers webauthn or totp and never this; the recovery screen is reachable only as a way OUT of one of those two, with a step id the person already holds.
waOff: webauthn.enabled is off, so no new security key can be enrolled here. It does not disable a key somebody already holds, for the TOTP row's reason — and there is a sharper edge: somebody whose only credential is a primary key would be locked out of their own account by this switch. Removing a key is on that person's row under
waRpIdSet: — configured. It is used only where it is a registrable domain suffix of the host this service was reached on; anything else is refused here, with the reason in the log, because a browser would refuse it with an error indistinguishable from a hardware failure.
waRpIdDefault: the host this service was reached on. That is the default and it is what a credential is bound to.
waRpName: — what a browser shows while somebody decides. It has no security meaning: WebAuthn binds a credential to the RP ID and to nothing else.
waUvEnforced: requested AND CHECKED. The UV flag is inside the bytes the authenticator signed, so an authenticator that did not verify the person is refused rather than quietly accepted. It is the only ceremony option on this page this service can check, because it is the only one anything signed says anything about.
waUvRequested: requested only. Nothing is refused on it.
waSentDirect: — and sent as direct, because this realm requires a trusted statement and a browser asked for less may strip it
waAttNext: . What is done with the statement is the next section.
waTimeout: {ms}ms, and it is a HINT: the specification lets a client clamp it and browsers do. The pending step this service holds expires on its own five-minute clock regardless.
waCtapNote: These three are what a browser translates into what it asks the AUTHENTICATOR for. They are requests and not checks: nothing signed says what the browser was asked for, so a check here would be a comparison against a value this service itself supplied. What this service does instead is RECORD what came back, beside the key.
waAttachAny: no preference sent, so any authenticator may answer — the member is omitted from the options rather than sent as a wide value, because the dictionary has no value meaning “any”
waAttachOnly: only. The browser filters; this service does not refuse a credential whose attachment turned out to be the other one.
waResident1: — a CTAP2 resident key, stored on the authenticator itself, for the sign-in screen's ceremony and Use a security key, decided by the
waResident2: (#527): required while usernameless sign-in is off, its securityKeyResidentKey while it is on. A passkey (Create a passkey) always asks required (#474): it is what the usernameless sign-in below finds. A resident key consumes one of the small number of slots a roaming authenticator has.
waCredPropsYes: asked for. It is the only way to find out whether a preferred ceremony actually produced a discoverable credential — nothing in the attestation says. The answer is recorded beside the key and decides nothing.
waCredPropsNo: not asked for, so nothing here knows whether an enrolled credential is discoverable.
waMayBeHeading: What a key may BE here
waMayBeNote: The three rows below are not WebAuthn. They are what THIS service will do with a key once the ceremony is over, decided here rather than by any specification — and all three refuse an enrolment and never an authentication. A key already on somebody's entry goes on working when the role that produced it is switched off.
waPrimaryYes: — a key may be the only credential on an account. The session then records amr ["hwk"] and acr "1".
waPrimaryNo: — the passwordless box is off the sign-in screen and the primary choice is off the portal.
waUsernamelessYes: — the sign-in screen draws Sign in with a passkey and its username field offers passkeys (autofill). The passkey names the account by its user handle, user verification is required, and the session records amr ["hwk","user"] and acr "mfa" (#474).
waNoPrimary: , and a primary key is not allowed
waUsernamelessNo3: . A passkey still signs in where the username is typed.
waMfaYes: — beside a password. The session then records amr ["pwd","hwk"] and acr "mfa".
waKeysPerPerson: {n}. Several is the ordinary case and the specification expects it: an assertion NAMES the credential that produced it, so there is none of the ambiguity two shared secrets would have.
waAlgNote: pubKeyCredParams is built from the OFFERED rows, in order. The list is filtered against what authn/webauthn.js can actually verify — a name outside that table is dropped with a warning rather than sent, because offering an algorithm this service cannot check produces a credential that enrols perfectly and then fails every assertion it is ever used for, at sign-in rather than at enrolment.
attPolicyOff: nothing is verified — the format is recorded and the statement believed. Development only.
attPolicyVerify: every statement that arrives is VERIFIED by its format's procedure and refused if it does not verify; a chain is checked against the anchors below, and a model the FIDO Metadata Service lists must chain to the roots it lists and is refused when MDS reports it compromised. none and self attestation are accepted as untrusted — which is what a synced passkey sends.
attPolicyRequire: only a statement that CHAINS TO AN ANCHOR is accepted: no none, no self attestation, and so no synced passkey.
attTrustAnyway: A trusted statement is required anyway, by the allow-list, certification level or FIPS rows below.
attFormats: — all eight of WebAuthn Level 3 section 8.
attAnchors: {n} configured (webauthn.attestationTrustAnchors), and the roots the FIDO Metadata Service lists for each model.
attMdsUnknown: not read in this process yet — the next draw has it.
attMdsStale: — STALE, so no model is known from it
attMdsNone: no BLOB is active, so no model's roots or status are known.
attSafetynetYes: trusted — deprecated, and Google no longer runs the service
attNote1: What a key's statement proved is on its row under
attNote2: and on /portal/keys: the format, whether it was verified and trusted, and the model the metadata names.
krbFromStored: a random key stored on the directory
krbFromUnreadable: a stored record this service cannot open — no TGT is issued
krbFromNothing: nothing yet — no TGT is issued
pkHeading: PKINIT: a certificate as the pre-authentication
pkFromCa: — from the Kerberos KDC Issuing CA on
pkNoCert: none yet in this process — issued on the first PKINIT request, with
pkTicketSays: the indicators pkinit, and pkinit-hardware with hw-authent for a smart-card logon certificate over a key this service never held; /authn/spnego reads them as swk and hwk, never pwd
thPasswordAlone: A password alone, for a person who holds or owes a second factor
krbPasswordRefused: — KDC_ERR_POLICY (12), only after the password verified; a wrong one is KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED as for anybody (product mode)
krbPasswordAccepted: — development mode issues a ticket on any password it accepts
krbFastYes: — armor FX_FAST_ARMOR_AP_REQUEST: a TGT the client host got with its own keytab (a service principal from
krbOtp: RFC 6560 OTP pre-authentication inside FAST: the password as the PIN and the person's authenticator app code, checked by the sign-in screen's own verifier and once-only step (kinit -T <armor ccache>). A smart-card or security-key certificate is PKINIT, below.
krbIndicator2: , carried into service tickets; /authn/spnego counts it as the second factor (amr pwd, otp; acr mfa)
perModeMemory: memory — nothing is written down. This is what this service did until 2026-08-27 and is still the default.
perFellBack2: . IT FELL BACK, which means the store could not be opened or read; the reason is below and in the log. Nothing is being written down. THIS SHOULD NOT BE REACHABLE: since 2026-08-28 a configured store that cannot be opened stops the process at startup rather than letting it run as something it is not, so a service drawing this page has one. Seeing it means something re-introduced the fallback — the row is kept as the net under that.
perLdif: — one RFC 2849 LDIF file per realm, plus realms.json and appconfig.json
perNeverShown: . The connection string itself is never shown here: it carries a password and this page is one fetch away from a log.
perNoCred: no connection is dialled, so there is no credential
perPwdFrom: — read once at startup and put into the connection string. The same mechanism, and by default the same file or secret, as the key-encryption key on
perPwdPlain: the connection string (persistence.databaseUrl), in plain text. persistence.databasePasswordProvider reads it from a mounted file, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault instead.
perTransportFile: a file on this machine — no connection, so nothing to encrypt
perTransportNone: nothing is written, so nothing is dialled
perWMinted: and everything this process mints — sessions, tokens, codes, artifacts, Kerberos principals, the replay caches, the counters and the audit log, across {stores} stores, every row encrypted
perNeverAll: everything — nothing at all is written in this mode
perNeverMinted: nothing, beyond the two caches that are re-derivable (the signed-metadata cache and the parsed-policy cache) and the plaintext of the signing keys, which are held encrypted. The private keys themselves are never written in the clear, and neither is any minted row.
perNeverList: sessions, access tokens, ID Tokens, refresh tokens, authorization codes, pre-authorized codes, SAML artifacts, Kerberos tickets, the replay caches, the statistics and the audit log
perBecauseDev: — because the signing key is regenerated on every start in development mode, so a token that outlived it would verify against nothing
perCoord: coordinating — applied up to change {seq}, {rows} row(s) taken from {others} other process(es), polling every {ms}ms with a LISTEN/NOTIFY nudge on top
perBehind: . This process is BEHIND and is serving its own copy until it catches up.
perNotCoord: not coordinating — this process holds its own copy and will not see another's writes until it restarts.
perCannot2: store cannot coordinate: a change log needs a transaction and a sequence, and that store writes whole files.
perImmediate: immediately — every change made while handling one request commits as one transaction the moment that request is done, plus a final flush on SIGTERM and SIGINT
perDelay: {ms}ms after a change, so a burst costs one file write, plus a final flush on SIGTERM and SIGINT. A kill -9 cannot be trapped and would lose up to that much.
perReadsAnswered: . Reads are still answered out of memory, and the write is retried on its own
per503: A request whose change was in it was answered 503 (LDAP: unavailable), never its success (#351).
perAnsweredBefore: The request that made the change was answered before it.
perAacYes: yes — a request that changed the store is answered once that change has committed, and 503 (LDAP: unavailable) when it has not
perAacNo: no — this store is written after the answer
perRefusedWaiting: A REFUSED WRITE IS WAITING FOR ITS RETRY
perHeld: ; writing requests are held for it.
perWorst: worst delay {max} ms since the last report
perWindow: , {max} ms in the window before it
perWrittenSoFar: {writes} flush(es), {failures} failure(s), {entries} entry/entries across {realms} realm(s). Last write
perPendingChange: ; a change is waiting to be written.
perRestored: {entries} directory entry/entries, {realms} trust realm(s) and {overrides} setting override(s), at
perRestoredZero: . Zero across the board means this was the first run against an empty store, which then had the seeded directory written into it.
perOffNote: Nothing on this page is in force: persistence.mode is memory, so this service is holding everything in memory and will lose all of it when the process ends — which is exactly what it has always done. The settings below change that, and all but one of them are restart-only, because the store is opened and READ before the listener binds.
perNotAccepting: The persistent store is not currently accepting writes. Everything below still describes what this service is trying to do; the Health row says what went wrong. Nothing has been lost — see the note above about a failed write.
